← Fireplace insert bid calculator

How much to charge to install a fireplace insert

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$2,499 installed” gas-insert special. That number is not a takeoff. A small gas cassette in an existing masonry firebox with a live stub, no liner, and a one-story stack is not the same job as a large wood insert with a 30-foot stainless liner, a new hearth pad, a surround, and a two-story chimney. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the liner and the extras, not just “an insert”

Chimney-sweep calculators price the flue, creosote, and CSIA height. A fireplace-insert hang is a different job: the unit, the liner, the hearth, and the extras that are not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published installed special is how the first seized damper eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each liner foot is time that never appears on the coupon. A hearth pad, a gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, and a damper are billed as their own hours. A two-story stack is an adder that gets forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a large wood insert with a 30-foot liner, a new hearth, a surround, a damper, tear-out, and second-story access prices about $14,882.94 (21.9 crew-hours). The same shop’s small gas brochure hang prices about $4,607.62 (7.0 hours, walk-away $3,133.18). Matching the $2,499 special already loses about $634 on the brochure hang, and it loses about $7,621 on the wood house — the walk-away on the heavy job is already $10,120.40.

Pellet and a short liner are not automatically a markup on gas

A medium pellet insert with a dedicated circuit, a 22-foot liner, and a new hearth is not the gas brochure hang plus 15%. On the sample rates that pellet job prices about $10,721.64 (16.7 crew-hours). A small gas hang with a 16-foot liner and a damper prices about $6,446.51 (10.7 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first seized damper.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $48/h installer loaded at 34% payroll burden is $64.32. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a fireplace design, a building-code determination, a permit, a WETT or CSIA inspection, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. The fuel, the opening, liner footage, hearth, gas, circuit, and finish are yours to confirm. It does not price a chimney sweep or a full chimney rebuild sold as the house.

Price your fireplace-insert hang

Common questions

How much to charge to install a fireplace insert?

Charge from the trip, the set, the liner or rebuild, the hearth, gas, circuit, surround, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default small gas insert in an existing firebox with a live stub, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $4,608 — about 7.0 crew-hours.

Why is a $2,499-installed fireplace-insert special dangerous?

Homeowners count an insert. Liner footage, a new hearth, a gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, and stack height do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a small gas hang is how a wood-and-liner job becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $2,499 special already loses about $634 against the $3,133 walk-away on the brochure hang, and it loses about $7,621 on the wood house whose walk-away is already $10,120.

How much to charge to install a wood fireplace insert with a liner?

A large wood insert with a 30-foot liner, a new hearth, and a surround is not a small gas special. On the sample rates that job prices around $14,883 (21.9 crew-hours), while a small gas brochure hang prices around $4,608 (7.0 hours).

Bid the liner, the hearth, and the stack.

Price a fireplace-insert install the way the trade actually loses money: liner footage, a new hearth, a gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, and a two-story stack. You get the bid, the hours the first liner actually consumes, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

The fireplace

Start from a common job, then replace every figure with your takeoff. Changing fuel, size, chimney, or access never overwrites a rate you already typed. This prices an insert hang — not a CSIA sweep, and not a full chimney rebuild sold as the house.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard or a fireplace design — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why can a competitor advertise “$2,499 installed”?

      Usually because the special is written around one specific job, and that job is a preset here: a small gas insert into an existing masonry firebox with a live gas stub already there, no liner needed, on a one-story stack. It really does price low. What the flat number cannot see is fuel type, liner footage, hearth work, a new gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, and stack height. Price your actual fireplace beside the special and the gap becomes a list of line items instead of an argument about who is honest.

      Why does a wood insert cost more to install than a gas insert of the same size?

      Mostly because of what has to happen above the firebox. A gas insert with an existing stub can skip the liner entirely. A wood-burning insert almost always needs a full stainless liner run to the top of the chimney for safe draft, priced by the linear foot — 30 feet on a tall stack is a very different job from 16 feet on a one-story house, even with the same size insert sitting in the firebox.

      Why does stack height change the price when the insert itself is identical?

      Because the liner run and the roof access both scale with the chimney, not the insert. A one-story stack with ground roof access is the cheap-special assumption. A two-story or unusually tall stack needs harder roof access and more liner footage to reach the top, and that access and material cost is separate from whatever insert gets set in the firebox.

      Is this the same as a chimney sweep or a full chimney rebuild?

      No. This prices installing the insert itself, the liner, the hearth, and the extras that go with it. It is distinct from a CSIA chimney sweep (cleaning the flue and clearing creosote, priced by flue height and condition) and from a full masonry chimney rebuild sold as its own job. A chimney that needs rebuilding before an insert can safely go in needs that work priced separately.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, a share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your fireplace details, wages, or prices.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — the insert, the liner, the hearth, the gas or electrical work, and the surround — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a price you are considering shows you the margin or the loss before you send it.

vs-a-flat-2499-installed-special.html.text:
← Fireplace Insert Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $2,499 installed special

"$2,499 installed" is not a price for a fireplace insert — it is a price for one specific firebox, quietly applied to every firebox that calls for a quote.

What a flat installed special is

A flat special is the fastest number a hearth shop can put on a postcard or a search ad: one price, no site visit, easy for a homeowner to compare between bids. It works for the shop as a lead magnet and works for the homeowner as a round number to shop around with. Nothing about the number says which firebox it was built for.

The number was set for one job — commonly a small gas cassette dropping into an existing masonry firebox that already has a gas stub, no liner needed, on a one-story stack — and then quoted to every caller afterward, whether or not the next firebox looks anything like the one the special was priced on.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the fuel type, insert size, chimney scope, liner footage, stack height, and flags for a new hearth, a gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, and a damper, plus your shop's wage, payroll burden, and target margin. It turns that into the crew hours the job actually consumes and a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this firebox, not the firebox the special was built on.

What a flat installed special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the job is a small gas cassette with an existing stub or a large wood insert needing a 30-foot liner, a new hearth, a surround, and a two-story stack. Prices fuel, liner footage, a new hearth, a gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, and stack access as their own lines, so a harder firebox returns a bigger number instead of the same one.
Has no line for a stainless liner run, a masonry rebuild, or a two-story stack — a straightforward gas hang prices the same as a wood insert needing a full reline. Bills liner footage by the foot, adds rebuild hours when the chimney needs one, and adds access hours for a two-story or tall stack only when that scope is turned on.
Was priced once, on one firebox, and never re-derived from a liner run, a hearth, or a fuel change — it is a marketing number, not a cost-basis number. Recomputes crew hours and material cost from the exact fuel, liner, hearth, and extras entered every time, so the price tracks the job rather than a memory of the postcard rate.
On this calculator's own small-gas-insert preset — the exact scope the special describes: existing stub, no liner, one-story stack — a $2,499 special still lands about $634.18 below the walk-away cost of the insert, tear-out, dump, permit, labor, and overhead alone, before any profit is counted. Returns a walk-away price of about $3,133.18 and a bid price of about $4,607.62 for that same small-gas job, at this tool's own shop-rate defaults and a 32% target margin.
On this calculator's own large-wood-insert preset — 30-foot liner, new hearth, surround, damper, two-story stack — a $2,499 special is about $7,621.40 below the walk-away cost, less than a quarter of what the job costs to deliver. Returns a walk-away price of about $10,120.40 and a bid price of about $14,882.94 for that same wood job, at the same defaults.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the crew hours behind it, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one firebox it was priced on, and nothing about a postcard rate tells a shop or a homeowner when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat special skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $2,499 installed special get fireplace inserts wrong?

Because the labor and materials an insert install needs come from the fuel type, the insert size, whether a liner has to run the full chimney, the hearth, a new gas or electrical run, a surround, and stack height — not from being "an insert." A small gas cassette dropping into an existing masonry firebox with a live gas stub and a large wood-burning insert needing a full 30-foot stainless liner, a new hearth pad, a surround, and a two-story stack are both "an insert," and a flat special charges them the same number.

What job is the $2,499 number actually built around?

One specific job: a small gas cassette going into an existing masonry firebox that already has a gas stub, needing no liner, on a one-story stack. It is a marketing price meant to get the phone to ring, not a number derived from any particular customer's fuel, liner run, or stack height.

Does the $2,499 number even cover the job it was named for?

On this calculator's own small-gas-insert preset — the exact scope the special describes: existing stub, no liner, one-story stack, priced at this tool's own shop-rate defaults — the walk-away cost of the insert, tear-out, dump, permit, labor, and overhead alone comes to about $3,133.18. A $2,499 special is already about $634.18 under that job's own break-even cost, before any profit is counted, on the easiest job it names.

What happens when the real job is a large wood insert instead?

On this calculator's own large-wood-insert preset — a 30-foot stainless liner, a new hearth pad, a surround, a damper, and a two-story stack, priced at this tool's own shop-rate defaults — the walk-away cost comes to about $10,120.40. A $2,499 special on that job is about $7,621.40 under the walk-away cost, less than a quarter of what the job costs to deliver before a dollar of profit.

Is a flat installed special ever the right way to quote?

For the one job the special was actually built around — a small gas cassette, existing stub, no liner, one-story stack — a flat number can land close, though this calculator's own defaults put even that job's break-even cost above $2,499. Outside that narrow scope, the gap between the special and the real cost grows fast, and neither the postcard nor the crew knows how far outside it a given firebox is until the fuel, liner, and stack are actually measured.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, insert prices, or what competitors advertise. It takes the wage, unit cost, and overhead you enter and turns them into a walk-away price for the fuel, liner, hearth, and access you describe — the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat installed special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest way to advertise that works until the firebox stops matching the one the special was priced on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $4,607.62, $3,133.18, $14,882.94, and $10,120.40 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on two worked jobs built into its own preset list (open the calculator and pick the small-gas or large-wood job from Starting job to reproduce them), not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs or any specific company's advertised price.

← Fireplace Insert Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this fireplace-insert job cost, given its fuel, liner footage, chimney scope, and access, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the fuel (gas, pellet, or wood), insert size, chimney scope (existing liner, new stainless liner, or a masonry rebuild), liner footage, roof access, and extras like a new hearth pad, a gas run, a dedicated circuit, a surround, or a damper, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a breakdown of where the hours and cost actually go, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
